entry: Chemical element, atomic number 19, symbol K. A silvery white [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]] soft enough to cut with a knife, potassium reacts rapidly with atmospheric oxygen and vigorously with water. It was first isolated in 1807 by [[Humphry Davy]] through [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]], and its name derives from [[Potash|potash]], the ashes of plants. Potassium is chemically similar to [[Sodium|sodium]], and most of its industrial uses exploit the high water solubility of its compounds. It occurs in many minerals, such as orthoclase, a common constituent of granites and other [[Igneous rock|igneous rocks]], and it is dissolved in seawater. Potassium ions are vital to all living cells, and both deficiency and excess can cause an abnormal heart rhythm. Agricultural [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]] containing potassium account for 95% of global potassium chemical production. Naturally occurring potassium includes radioactive 40K, the most common radioisotope in the human body.

Metal halide salt of potassium and chlorine (KCl). It is odorless, forms white or colorless crystals, and dissolves readily in water, with a salt-like taste. It occurs naturally as the [[Mineral|mineral]] sylvite and with [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]] as sylvinite. Most production goes to [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]], sold as [[Potash|muriate of potash]] because the growth of many plants is limited by potassium availability. It is also used as a salt substitute, as a [[Medication|medication]], and in oral rehydration solutions to reduce low blood potassium caused by diarrhea. It is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines.

Highly toxic salt (KCN), similar in appearance to sugar and highly soluble in water. Most of it is used in gold mining, organic synthesis and electroplating. A dose of 200 to 300 milligrams will kill nearly any human. The moist solid releases small amounts of [[Hydrogen cyanide|hydrogen cyanide]] through hydrolysis, a gas often described as smelling of bitter almonds. Before 1900 it was the most important source of [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]] cyanides. It is also used as a photographic fixer in the wet plate collodion process.

Inorganic compound (KOH), commonly called caustic potash. Along with [[Sodium hydroxide|sodium hydroxide]] (NaOH), it is a prototypical strong base with many industrial and niche applications, most of which exploit its caustic nature and reactivity toward acids. About 2.5 million tonnes were produced in 2023. It is the precursor to most soft and liquid [[Soap|soaps]] and to numerous potassium-containing chemicals. The white solid is hygroscopic and dangerously corrosive. About 112 g dissolve in 100 mL of water at room temperature, slightly more than sodium hydroxide, and its affinity for water makes it a laboratory desiccant, especially for drying [[Amine|amines]] and pyridines. Since the late 19th century it has largely been made by electrolysis of [[Potassium chloride|potassium chloride]] solutions.

Ionic compound (KI), used as a medication and dietary supplement. In radiation emergencies it protects the [[Thyroid|thyroid]] gland by blocking uptake of radioactive iodine. It is also used to treat hyperthyroidism and as a supplement for people with low dietary intake of iodine. Common side effects include vomiting, [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], abdominal pain and rash. It has been used medically since at least 1820 and is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines. Its most common use as a food additive is iodizing table salt.

Potassium salt of nitric acid (KNO₃), an alkali metal nitrate. It occurs naturally as the mineral niter, one of several nitrogen-containing compounds called saltpeter. It is a source of [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]], and nitrogen was named after niter. Its major uses are in [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], rocket propellants and fireworks. It is one of the main constituents of traditional [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]], and in processed meats it reacts with hemoglobin to generate a red color. Historically, natural sources included cave deposits and bat [[Guano|guano]]. In 1270 Hasan al-Rammah of [[Syria]] outlined a purification process that used wood ashes to remove calcium and magnesium.

Purplish-black crystalline salt (KMnO₄), a strong oxidizing agent. It dissolves in water to give an intensely pink to purple solution. It is widely used in the [[Chemical industry|chemical industry]] and in laboratories, and traditionally as a medication for dermatitis, for cleaning [[Wound|wounds]] and for general disinfection. It is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines, but it should never be taken internally, because it is highly toxic and corrosive. Other uses include water treatment and dyeing cloth. Its nicknames include Condy's crystals and chameleon mineral.

Energy an object or system has because of its position relative to other objects, or the configuration of its particles. It equals the work done against restoring forces, such as [[Gravity|gravity]] or those in a [[Spring (device)|spring]]. The term was introduced by the Scottish engineer and physicist William Rankine, who coined it in 1853, though it has links to [[Aristotle|Aristotle]]'s concept of potentiality. Common types include gravitational potential energy, the elastic potential energy of a deformed spring, and the electric potential energy of an [[Electric charge|electric charge]] in an electric field. Potential energy is associated with conservative forces, whose total [[Work (physics)|work]] depends only on the initial and final positions. Its SI unit is the [[Joule|joule]] (J). For a mass m at height h above a reference point, gravitational potential energy is Ug = mgh. Potential energy can be converted into [[Kinetic energy|kinetic energy]] as an object falls or a spring releases.

Machine used to shape round ceramic ware from [[Clay|clay]]. In throwing, a lump of clay is centered on the wheel and squeezed, lifted and shaped as the wheel turns. The wheel is also used to trim excess clay from leather-hard ware and to apply decoration. Its use spread widely across the Old World, but it was unknown in the pre-Columbian New World, where [[Pottery|pottery]] was handmade by coiling and beating. Early slow wheels, called tournettes, were in use around 3500 BC in the Near East. The fast wheel, which stores energy in a heavy flywheel, was developed in the mid to late 3rd millennium BC. Many scholars suggest it was first developed by the [[Sumer|Sumerians]] of [[Mesopotamia]], where a stone wheel found at [[Ur]] has been dated to about 3129 BC.

Domesticated birds raised for meat, eggs or feathers. Poultry are mostly members of the superorder Galloanserae, especially the order [[Galliformes]], which includes [[Chicken|chickens]] and [[Turkey (bird)|turkeys]], and the family Anatidae, which includes [[Duck|ducks]] and geese. Recent genomic studies date chicken domestication to around 8,000 years ago in [[Southeast Asia]]. Selective breeding for fast growth, egg-laying and docility has produced breeds that often look very different from their wild ancestors, and most birds on the market are reared in intensive commercial enterprises. Together with [[Pork|pork]], poultry is one of the two most widely eaten meats globally, with over 70% of the meat supply in 2012 between them. Its meat provides high-quality protein with little fat. Poultry is distinct from game, which consists of wild birds hunted for food or sport.

Unit of mass in the British imperial and United States customary systems. The most common modern definition is the international avoirdupois pound, legally defined as exactly 0.45359237 kg and divided into 16 avoirdupois ounces. The United States and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] agreed on this definition in 1959, and the United Kingdom implemented it in the Weights and Measures Act 1963. The name descends from the Roman libra, which is the origin of the symbol lb. The United States is the only industrialized country where commercial activity does not predominantly use the [[Metric system|metric system]], and the pound remains widely used there. Because the unqualified term reflects a historical conflation of mass and weight, the terms pound-mass and pound-force distinguish the two.

[[Currency|Currency]] of the [[United Kingdom]] and several dependent territories (symbol £, code GBP). Each pound has been divided into 100 pence since 1971. Sterling is the world's oldest currency in continuous use. In 2025 it was the fourth most traded currency in the foreign exchange market, after the [[United States dollar|U.S. dollar]], the [[Euro|euro]] and the [[Japanese yen]]. The Bank of England issues banknotes in England and Wales and regulates the notes issued by private banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland. The name is traced to the silver penny, or sterling, of medieval England, of which 240 made a pound of sterlings. The symbol £ derives from the Latin libra, the abbreviation for the Roman pound.

American media franchise centered on a [[Superhero|superhero]] television series. The first entry, *Mighty Morphin Power Rangers*, debuted on August 28, 1993, and adapts characters and footage from the Japanese tokusatsu franchise Super Sentai. Teams of youths morph into Rangers who pilot Zords that combine into a Megazord. Despite criticism from parents and watchdogs that its violence was unsuitable for children, the franchise generated over $6 billion in toy sales by 2001. In 2018 Bandai parted ways with the franchise, and Hasbro acquired it.

Amount of energy transferred or converted per unit time. In the International System of Units, the unit of power is the watt (W), equal to one [[Joule|joule]] per second. Power is a scalar quantity. Mechanical power is the product of force and [[Velocity|velocity]], or of [[Torque|torque]] and angular velocity for a rotating shaft, and electrical power is the product of current and [[Voltage|voltage]]. Average power is the work done divided by the time interval, and instantaneous power is its limit as that interval approaches zero. Other units include [[Horsepower|horsepower]], equal to about 745.7 watts. Burning a kilogram of [[Coal|coal]] releases more energy than detonating a kilogram of [[TNT]], but TNT delivers more power because it releases energy more quickly.

Industrial facility for generating electric power, generally connected to an electrical grid. Most power stations contain [[Electric generator|generators]], rotating machines that convert mechanical power into three-phase electric power through the relative motion of a magnetic field and a conductor. Most of the world's stations burn fossil fuels such as [[Coal|coal]], oil and natural gas, while low-carbon sources include [[Nuclear power|nuclear power]] and renewables such as solar, wind and hydroelectric. In September 1882 Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station began supplying electric lighting in New York using direct current. In 1886 George Westinghouse began building an alternating current system that used a transformer to step voltage up for long-distance transmission, and AC distribution eventually prevailed. Fossil-fuel stations emit [[Sulfur dioxide|sulfur dioxide]] and [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], contributing to acid rain and climate change.

Electrical device that supplies power to a load by converting current from a source to the required [[Voltage|voltage]], current and frequency. Sources include the grid, batteries, fuel cells, generators and solar converters. Power supplies may also limit the [[Electric current|current]] drawn by the load, shut off current during a fault, filter noise and surges from the input, and store energy as an uninterruptible power supply. Regulated supplies keep output voltage or current constant despite changes in load or input, while unregulated supplies do not. Linear supplies produce clean, low-noise output but waste energy as heat, whereas switching supplies convert the input into pulses and are generally more efficient and smaller. An external supply, or power brick, sits in the load's cord and steps hazardous mains voltage down to a safer level.

Competitive strength sport of three maximal attempts in the squat, bench press and deadlift. Like [[Olympic weightlifting|Olympic weightlifting]], it involves single maximal lifts with a loaded barbell. Powerlifting evolved from a sport called odd lifts, which used more events and was later standardized to the current three. Lifts may be equipped, using supportive bench shirts or squat suits, or unequipped, called raw or classic lifting. The modern sport originated in the [[United Kingdom]] and the [[United States]] in the 1950s, and the first named U.S. national championships were held in 1965. The International Powerlifting Federation was founded in 1972. Powerlifting has been a Paralympic sport, for bench press only, since 1984.

Largest freshwater lake in China, in Jiangxi Province. Fed by the Gan, Xin and Xiu rivers, it flows northward through a channel into the [[Yangtze|Yangtze River]]. Its area fluctuates seasonally: in a normal year it averages 3,500 sq km (1,400 sq mi), but in early 2012 drought, sand quarrying and water storage at the [[Three Gorges Dam]] reduced it to about 200 sq km. The lake provides habitat for half a million migratory birds, and in winter it hosts up to 90% of the critically endangered Siberian crane species. Sand dredging and heavy shipping have endangered the finless porpoise, of which about 1,400 were left in 2007. A 10-year fishing moratorium on 332 sites along the Yangtze, including the lake, was imposed in January 2020.

City on the Warta River in western [[Poland]], capital of Greater Poland Voivodeship. Poznań is the fifth-largest city in Poland, and its metropolitan area has more than one million inhabitants. One of four historical capitals of medieval Poland, it is an important center of trade, sports, education and tourism, and home to [[Adam Mickiewicz|Adam Mickiewicz University]]. It is the seat of Poland's oldest diocese and hosts the Poznań International Fair, the biggest industrial fair in Poland. Its early stronghold, on what is now Ostrów Tumski, was an important center of the Western Polans, and [[Mieszko I]]'s [[Baptism|baptism]] in AD 966 may have taken place there. In June 1956, workers at the Cegielski factories protested against communist economic policies, and the clashes that followed claimed dozens of lives.

Indian actor who works mainly in Telugu cinema. Known in the media as Rebel Star, he is one of the highest-paid actors in Indian cinema. His breakthrough came with the action romance *Varsham* (2004). He starred in the epic duology *Baahubali: The Beginning* (2015) and *Baahubali 2: The Conclusion* (2017), the latter the highest-grossing Indian film at that point, and became the first pan-Indian star. Later films include *Saaho* (2019), *Salaar: Part 1 – Ceasefire* (2023) and *Kalki 2898 AD* (2024). He is the first Indian actor to have a film gross over ₹1000 crore worldwide.

Indonesian politician and retired military officer, eighth president of Indonesia since 2024. He is the country's third president with a military background, after [[Suharto|Suharto]] and Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono. He served in the Special Forces (Kopassus) and led the Strategic Reserves Command (Kostrad) before being discharged in 1998. He ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 2014 and 2019, then served as minister of defense from 2019 to 2024. As president he launched the sovereign wealth fund Danantara and oversaw Indonesia's entry to [[BRICS]].

Branch of [[Linguistics|linguistics]] and [[Semiotics|semiotics]] that studies how context contributes to meaning. Pragmatics covers implicature, speech acts, relevance, conversation and nonverbal communication, and it is closely linked to [[Semantics|semantics]] and [[Syntax|syntax]]. Charles Morris first distinguished it as a separate subfield in 1938, alongside syntax and semantics. It emerged as its own subfield in the 1950s through the work of J. L. Austin and Paul Grice. Austin's speech act theory holds that utterances can perform actions, such as apologizing, and John Searle later developed a taxonomy of speech act types. Grice's cooperative principle explains conversational implicatures, meanings inferred when speakers flout maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner.

Philosophical tradition that views language and thought as tools for prediction, problem solving and action. It began in the United States in the 1870s, with origins often attributed to [[Charles Sanders Peirce|Charles Sanders Peirce]], [[William James]] and [[John Dewey]]. In 1878 Peirce stated his pragmatic maxim, which holds that a conception's meaning is the whole of its conceivable practical effects. James first used the name in print in 1898 and credited Peirce with coining it. Dewey developed the approach into instrumentalism, viewing ideas as tools for solving problems. Pragmatists contend that knowledge, meaning and belief are best understood through practical use and success. The tradition influenced [[Analytic philosophy|analytic philosophy]] and education, and Richard Rorty later adapted it into neopragmatism.

Period of political liberalization in [[Czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]], from January to August 1968. Reformist [[Alexander Dubček]] was elected First Secretary of the Communist Party in January 1968 and loosened restrictions on the media, speech and travel, while partly decentralizing the economy. On August 21, 1968, the [[Soviet Union]] and four other [[Warsaw Pact]] members invaded with about half a million troops to suppress the reforms. Resistance was largely nonviolent and held out for almost eight months until diplomatic maneuvers ended it. Under normalization, Gustáv Husák reversed almost all of the reforms. The 1989 Velvet Revolution peacefully ended the communist regime.

Capital and largest city of the [[Czech Republic]], on the Vltava River (pop., 2025: 1,396,886). Prague is the historical capital of [[Bohemia]] and was a residence of several Holy Roman Emperors, notably Charles IV, under whom Charles University was founded in 1348. Charles University is the oldest university in Central Europe. The city was part of the [[Habsburg monarchy]], played major roles in the Bohemian and Protestant Reformations and the [[Thirty Years' War]], and was capital of Czechoslovakia between the world wars. Its historic center, with Prague Castle, Charles Bridge and the Old Town astronomical clock, has been a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site since 1992. In 2017 it received more than 8.5 million international visitors.
